rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: ʿĀṣim reads jadhwa with fatḥa, Ḥamza and Khalaf with ḍamma, and the rest with kasra; these are three dialectal forms.
rows.anchor: قرأ عاصم أو جذوة بفتح الجيم

rows.speaker: الحسن
rows.claim: In a noncanonical reading, al-Ḥasan reads al-ajalayni with lightened, vowelless yāʾ.
rows.anchor: قراءة الحسن الأجلين بتخفيف الياء وسكونها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Jadhwa is thick firewood containing fire; its plural is jadhā, illustrated by an unattributed line.
rows.anchor: الجذوة القطعة الغليظة من الحطب فيها النار

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Shāṭiʾ is a valley’s side or bank, also called al-shaṭṭ; its plural is shawāṭiʾ.
rows.anchor: وشاطئ الوادي جانبه وهو الشط والجمع الشواطئ

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Hātayn qualifies bintay; thamāni ḥijaj is a temporal adverb, and dhalika is a subject with baynī wa-baynak as predicate.
rows.anchor: هاتين صفة لابنتي. ثماني حجج ظرف زمان

rows.speaker: الزجاج
rows.claim: Al-Zajjāj explains the agreement as reciprocal: what Moses stipulated is his, what the employer stipulated is his.
rows.anchor: ومعناه ما شرطت علي فلك وما شرطت لي فلي

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ayy is conditional and governed as an object by qaḍaytu; mā is emphatic and the answer is fa-lā ʿudwāna ʿalayya.
rows.anchor: وأي في معنى الجزاء وهي منصوبة بقضيت

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The particle before “O Moses” is an accusative, lightened form of inna, with an understood “that” clause.
rows.anchor: أن في موضع نصب وهي مخففة من الثقيلة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The daughter who married Moses was Ṣaffūra and the other Layyā; another account names the elder Ṣafrāʾ and younger Ṣafīrāʾ.
rows.anchor: وهي التي تزوج بها واسم الأخرى ليا

words: إِنَّ خَيْرَ مَنِ ٱسْتَـْٔجَرْتَ ٱلْقَوِىُّ ٱلْأَمِينُ
rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The best person to hire is strong enough to do the work and trustworthy in carrying it out.
rows.anchor: خير من استعملت من قوي على العمل وإداء الأمانة

rows.speaker: عمر بن الخطاب
rows.claim: ʿUmar says Shuʿayb asked how his daughter knew Moses was strong and trustworthy: he lifted a massive stone, then asked her to walk behind him so the wind would not reveal her body.
rows.anchor: قال عمر بن الخطاب: لما قالت المرأة هذا

rows.speaker: قيل
rows.claim: Another explanation says Moses was strong because he drew the well’s stone, which only a group could lift, and trustworthy because he lowered his gaze while watering for the women.
rows.anchor: وقيل: القوي في نزعه الحجر من البئر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Shuʿayb offers one daughter in marriage for eight years of work; completing ten is voluntary generosity, not an obligation.
rows.anchor: أي على أن تكون أجيرا لي ثماني سنين

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: One view makes the service the marriage payment; another says Shuʿayb paid a dowry and separately hired Moses for shepherding. The latter fits Abū Ḥanīfa’s school, but service-as-dowry better fits the verse’s surface sense.
rows.anchor: وقيل: معناه على أن تجعل جزائي وثوابي إياك

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Shuʿayb will not burden Moses with duties beyond tending sheep; alternatively, he will not force Moses to complete ten years.
rows.anchor: في هذه الثمانية حجج وأن أكلفك خدمة سوى رعي الغنم

words: سَتَجِدُنِىٓ إِن شَآءَ ٱللَّهُ مِنَ ٱلصَّٰلِحِينَ
rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Shuʿayb conditions his good companionship and fidelity on God’s will because his survival is uncertain and God may take him before he can act rightly.
rows.anchor: إنما علق الصلاح بمشيئة الله لأن مراده

rows.speaker: يحيى بن سلام
rows.claim: Yaḥyā ibn Sallām relates that Moses was allotted each sheep skin set against its mother’s coloring; God then inspired him in a dream to cast his staff into water, after which all lambs bore opposite markings.
rows.anchor: وحكى يحيى بن سلام أنه جعل لموسى كل سلخة

rows.speaker: ابن عباس وغيره
rows.claim: A report invoked alongside the verse says Abū Ṭālib did not accept Islam while Waḥshī did; it is transmitted from Ibn ʿAbbās and others.
rows.anchor: فلم يسلم أبو طالب وأسلم وحشي ورووا ذلك عن ابن عباس وغيره

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Prophet cannot will something contrary to God’s will, just as he cannot disobey God’s commands and prohibitions.
rows.anchor: فإن النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم لا يجوز أن يخالف الله سبحانه في إرادته

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The account would make the Prophet want Abū Ṭālib’s faith while God wills his unbelief, yet the Prophet would dislike Waḥshī’s faith while God wills it; this entails an untenable conflict.
rows.anchor: فقد حصل غاية الخلاف بين إرادتي الرسول صلى الله عليه وسلم والمرسل

rows.speaker: قيل
rows.claim: The people do not know or worship God and thus do not recognize the reward they are missing.
rows.anchor: لا يعلمون الله ولا يعبدونه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “How many a town” means how many of a town’s inhabitants were destroyed.
rows.anchor: أي من أهل قرية

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: They received broad provision but failed to thank God for it and grew arrogant, so they were destroyed.
rows.anchor: أعطيناهم المعيشة الواسعة فلم يعرفوا حق النعمة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The dwellings are those of ʿĀd in al-Aḥqāf between Yemen and Syria, Thamūd in Wādī al-Qurā, and Lot’s people at Sodom; Meccans knew them from trade journeys.
rows.anchor: تلك إشارة إلى ما يعرفونه هم من ديار عاد وثمود وقوم لوط

words: لَمْ تُسْكَن مِّنۢ بَعْدِهِمْ إِلَّا قَلِيلًۭا
rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Their homes became vacant of inhabitants, with little later occupancy.
rows.anchor: صارت مساكنهم خاوية خالية عن أهلها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God is the heir because He owns their dwellings and no one succeeded them there.
rows.anchor: أي المالكين لديارهم لم يخلفهم أحد فيها

rows.speaker: قيل
rows.claim: One interpretation takes the town’s “mother” to mean Mecca, Umm al-Qurā.
rows.anchor: قيل أن معنى أمها أم القرى وهي مكة

rows.speaker: قيل
rows.claim: Another interpretation takes the town’s “mother” to mean the principal town among the world’s settlements.
rows.anchor: وقيل: يريد معظم القرى من سائر الدنيا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God sends a messenger to the central town to recite His proofs and clear signs before destroying towns.
rows.anchor: أي يقرأ عليهم حججنا وبيناتنا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Destruction comes only when residents wrong themselves through unbelief, transgression, arrogance, and disobedience.
rows.anchor: لنفوسهم بالكفر والطغيان والعتو والعصيان

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Whatever people receive is worldly enjoyment and adornment; God’s reward and the afterlife are better and more enduring because worldly goods perish.
rows.anchor: أي وما أعطيتموه من شيء

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The closing question urges reflection to distinguish what lasts from what passes away.
rows.anchor: حتى تميزوا بين الباقي والفاني

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Qatāda reports that the command to dispute graciously was abrogated by the Sword Verse; al-Ṭabrisī rejects abrogation because gracious disputation is obligatory.
rows.anchor: عن قتادة والصحيح أنها غير منسوخة

words: آمَنَّا بِٱلَّذِىٓ أُنزِلَ إِلَيْنَا وَأُنزِلَ إِلَيْكُمْ
rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: In inviting the People of the Book, believers should affirm the scripture sent to both communities.
rows.anchor: أي بالكتاب الذي أنزل إلينا وبالكتاب الذي أنزل إليكم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Their shared God is one without a partner, and believers are sincere and obedient to Him.
rows.anchor: لا شريك له { ونحن له مسلمون } أي مخلصون طائعون

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: As scripture was sent to Moses and Jesus, the Qurʾān was sent to Muhammad.
rows.anchor: أي ومثل ما أنزلنا الكتاب على موسى وعيسى

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “Those given the Book” can mean believing People of the Book, such as ʿAbd Allāh ibn Salām; “these” can mean Meccans who converted, and “it” can refer to the Prophet or Qurʾān.
rows.anchor: يعني مؤمني أهل الكتاب مثل عبد الله بن سلام ونظرائه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Alternatively, those given the Book are Muslims and the Book is the Qurʾān; “these” then means Jews and Christians, some of whom believe in it.
rows.anchor: ويحتمل أيضا أن يريد بقوله الذين آتيناهم الكتاب المسلمين

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Only unbelievers reject God’s signs, and their denial does not harm the Prophet.
rows.anchor: وما ينكر دلالاتنا إلا الكافرون ولا يضرك جحودهم

words: وَمَا كُنتَ تَتْلُوا۟ مِن قَبْلِهِۦ مِن كِتَٰبٍۢ
rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Before revelation, Muhammad neither read nor wrote a book; he did not know how to read before receiving the Qurʾān.
rows.anchor: وما كنت يا محمد تقرأ قبل القرآن كتابا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Had he read or written beforehand, false claimants could accuse him of compiling earlier books and cast doubt among the weak.
rows.anchor: ولقالوا: إنما تقرأ علينا ما جمعته من كتب الأولين

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: His inimitable account of earlier peoples, though he grew among people who watched him and saw no teacher, shows the Qurʾān came from God.
rows.anchor: ثم أتيت بما عجزوا عنه وجب أن يعلموا أنه من عند الله

words: وَمَا كُنتَ تَتْلُوا۟ مِن قَبْلِهِۦ مِن كِتَٰبٍۢ
rows.speaker: الشريف الأجل المرتضى
rows.claim: Al-Murtaḍā says the Prophet was not literate before prophethood; after it, either literacy or continued illiteracy is possible, and the verse does not decide.
rows.anchor: قال الشريف الأجل المرتضى علم الهدى قدس الله روحه:

rows.speaker: الشريف الأجل المرتضى
rows.claim: Al-Murtaḍā says the negation concerns only the time before prophethood, since prior literacy would invite suspicion; after revelation, Gabriel could have taught him.
rows.anchor: قال الشريف الأجل المرتضى علم الهدى قدس الله روحه:

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ibn Kathīr, Qālūn, and Kufans except ʿĀṣim, al-Aʿmash, and al-Burjumī read the lām vowelless; the rest read it with kasra.
rows.anchor: قرأ ابن كثير وقالون وأهل الكوفة غير عاصم

rows.speaker: أبو علي
rows.claim: With kasra, the lām is purposive and attaches to associating: they associate only to disbelieve and enjoy worldly life, with no share in the afterlife. The vowelless reading is an imperative of threat, like 17:64 and 41:40.
rows.anchor: قال أبو علي: من كسر اللام وجعلها الجارة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ibn Kathīr reads āteytum with a short alif; the others lengthen it.
rows.anchor: قرأ ابن كثير { ما آتيتم من ربا } مقصورة الألف غير ممدودة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Medinese readers, Yaʿqūb, and Sahl read li-turbū with tāʾ, ḍamma, and still wāw; the rest read li-yarbū with yāʾ, fatḥa, and accusative wāw.
rows.anchor: وقرأ أهل المدينة ويعقوب وسهل لتربوا بالتاء وضمها وسكون الواو

rows.speaker: أبو علي
rows.claim: Riba can be a gift offered in expectation of a larger return; it does not grow with God because the giver sought compensation, not God’s favor.
rows.anchor: ما آتيتم من هدية أهديتموها لتعوضوا ما هو أكثر منه

rows.speaker: أبو علي
rows.claim: The long reading means “you gave”; the short reading can mean “you did” or “came to,” as ordinary usage for performing an act.
rows.anchor: فمن مد آتيتم فلأن المعنى أعطيتم

rows.speaker: أبو علي
rows.claim: A poem, “أتيت الذي يأتي السفيه,” uses atā for doing what a fool does, illustrating how the short reading can describe an act.
rows.anchor: قال الشاعر: أتيت الذي يأتي السفيه

rows.speaker: أبو علي
rows.claim: All readers lengthen āteytum in the zakāt phrase, as in “giving zakāt” at 21:73; ordinary usage and scripture favor the long form.
rows.anchor: ولم يختلفوا في مد وما آتيتم من زكوة

rows.speaker: أبو علي
rows.claim: For li-yarbū, the subject is the previously mentioned riba, with an omitted genitive: it is meant to grow by attracting people’s wealth.
rows.anchor: ومن قرأ ليربو فإن فاعله الربا المذكور

rows.speaker: أبو علي
rows.claim: The gift itself is not legally riba; the prohibited excess is what is taken above the principal. A gift seeking return is named for its intended increase.
rows.anchor: والمدفوع ليس في الحقيقة ربا إنما المحرم الزيادة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The idolaters rejoice when given health, bodily well-being, ample provision, security, or ease.
rows.anchor: أي إذا آتيناهم نعمة من عافية وصحة جسم أو سعة رزق

words: وَإِن تُصِبْهُم سَيِّئَةٌۢ بِمَا قَدَّمَتْ أَيْدِيهِمْ
rows.speaker: الجبائي
rows.claim: Al-Jubbāʾī says adversity is punishment for sins; calling it a misfortune is figurative because it repays wrongdoing.
rows.anchor: عن الجبائي

rows.speaker: قيل
rows.claim: Another view identifies adversity as drought, stopped rain, and hardship, called misfortune because it troubles the recipient.
rows.anchor: وقيل: وإن يصبهم قحط وانقطاع مطر وشدة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: When hardship strikes, they despair of God’s mercy.
rows.anchor: أي ييأسون من رحمة الله

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “Their hands have sent ahead” stands for deeds because hands commonly perform work; heart deeds may be many but hidden.
rows.anchor: فإن أكثر العمل لليدين والعمل للقلب

words: أَوَلَمْ يَرَوْا أَنَّ ٱللَّهَ يَبْسُطُ ٱلرِّزْقَ
rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God expands or restricts provision according to what benefits His servants; this is a sign for believers.
rows.anchor: على حسب ما تقتضيه مصالح العباد

rows.speaker: مجاهد والسدي
rows.claim: Mujāhid and al-Suddī say the kin’s due means rights God assigned Muhammad’s relatives from the khums.
rows.anchor: حقوقهم التي جعلها الله لهم من الأخماس عن مجاهد والسدي

rows.speaker: أبو سعيد الخدري وغيره
rows.claim: Abū Saʿīd al-Khudrī and others report that when the verse came down, the Prophet gave Fadak to Fāṭima; the account is also transmitted from Abū Jaʿfar and Abū ʿAbd Allāh.
rows.anchor: وروى أبو سعيد الخدري وغيره أنه لما نزلت هذه الآية

rows.speaker: الحسن
rows.claim: Al-Ḥasan says this addresses the Prophet and everyone: each person’s kin are meant, to be supported with wealth and personal help.
rows.anchor: عن الحسن

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The needy and stranded traveler are to receive the dues God assigned them in one’s wealth.
rows.anchor: والمسافر المحتاج ما فرض الله لهم في مالك

words: ذَٰلِكَ خَيْرٌۭ لِّلَّذِينَ يُرِيدُونَ وَجْهَ ٱللَّهِ
rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Giving people their due is good for those seeking God’s face rather than display or reputation, and they are successful.
rows.anchor: بالإعطاء دون الرياء والسمعة

rows.speaker: ابن عباس وطاوس
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAbbās and Ṭāwūs, and a report from Abū Jaʿfar, treat this as lawful gift-giving in hope of a larger return, without reward or sin.
rows.anchor: عن ابن عباس وطاوس

rows.speaker: الحسن والجبائي
rows.claim: Al-Ḥasan and al-Jubbāʾī identify the riba as prohibited interest, as in 2:276.
rows.anchor: والقول الآخر: أنه الربا المحرم عن الحسن والجبائي

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Nāfiʿ reads li-turbū; other readers read li-yarbū with different person, vowels, and inflection.
rows.anchor: وقول نافع لتربوا أي لتصيروا ذوي زيادة

rows.speaker: نافع
rows.claim: Nāfiʿ’s reading means becoming possessors of increase from other people’s wealth, seeking and attracting it, as in arbā.
rows.anchor: أي تستدعونها وتجتلبونها وكأنه من أربى

words: وَمَآ ءَاتَيْتُم مِّن زَكَوٰةٍۢ تُرِيدُونَ وَجْهَ ٱللَّهِ
rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Zakat given to rightful recipients seeking God’s reward and approval, not repayment, makes its givers people whose reward is multiplied.
rows.anchor: أي وما أعطيتموه أهله على وجه الزكاة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: One explanation is people possessing multiplied good deeds, as a person may be described as possessing strength or wealth.
rows.anchor: وقيل: المضعفون ذوو الإضعاف في الحسنات

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Another explanation is increased wealth in this life and reward in the next, since God made zakat a cause of increased wealth.
rows.anchor: وقيل: هم المضعفون للمال في العاجل وللثواب في الآجل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A Prophetic report says that charity does not diminish wealth.
rows.anchor: ما نقص مال من صدقة

rows.speaker: أمير المؤمنين
rows.claim: ʿAlī says prayer cleanses arrogance, zakat brings provision, fasting tests sincerity, and kinship ties increase numbers, in a longer discourse.
rows.anchor: وقال أمير المؤمنين ع: فرض الله تعالى الصلاة تنزيها عن الكبر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The verse shifts from direct address to reported statement, a feature counted among forms of eloquence.
rows.anchor: وبدأ سبحانه في الآية بالخطاب ثم ثنى بالخبر

words: ٱللَّهُ ٱلَّذِى خَلَقَكُمْ ثُمَّ رَزَقَكُمْ ثُمَّ يُمِيتُكُمْ ثُمَّ يُحْيِيكُمْ
rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God creates, provides, causes death, then raises people to recompense their actions.
rows.anchor: { ثم يحييكم } ليجازيكم على أفعالكم

words: هَلْ مِن شُرَكَآئِكُم مَّن يَفْعَلُ مِن ذَٰلِكُم مِّن شَىْءٍ
rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: No partner can do these things or merit worship on that basis; God is exalted above their association.
rows.anchor: ثم نزه سبحانه نفسه عن أن يشرك معه في العبادة

rows.speaker: زيد
rows.claim: Zayd reads awalam nahdi with nūn; all other readers use yāʾ. It was also discussed in Sūrat al-Aʿrāf.
rows.anchor: قرأ زيد أو لم نهد بالنون

rows.speaker: ابن السميفع
rows.claim: In noncanonical readings, Ibn al-Sumayfa reads yamshūn with passive yāʾ and doubled shīn; he reads muntazirūn with fatḥa on ẓāʾ.
rows.anchor: قراءة ابن السميفع يمشون بضم الياء وتشديد الشين

rows.speaker: أبو حاتم
rows.claim: Abū Ḥātim rejects fatḥa on ẓāʾ, arguing from “So watch; they too are watching.”
rows.anchor: دفع أبو حاتم فتح الظاء

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The plural reading is explained as indicating abundance; a cited, unattributed line uses the verb in the singular.
rows.anchor: وقوله يمشون للكثرة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Guidance includes what a person cannot do without in religion; divine grace and reasoning that leads to knowledge of God are both guidance.
rows.anchor: والواجب من الهدى هو ما يؤدي إلى ما ليس للعبد عنه غنى

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Sūq means urging or driving along; sāqahu yasūquhu means he drove it.
rows.anchor: والسوق الحث على السير ساقه يسوقه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-jurz is dry, plantless land after rain ceases; its root is linked to cutting and to a voracious eater. Four vowel patterns are listed, with a rajaz verse illustrating jarūz.
rows.anchor: الجزر الأرض اليابسة التي ليس فيها نبات لانقطاع الأمطار عنها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The subject of yahdi is implicit, supplied by “how many We destroyed”; kam is the object of ahlaknā, and yamshūn is circumstantial.
rows.anchor: فاعل يهد مضمر يدل عليه قوله

words: كَمْ أَهْلَكْنَا مِن قَبْلِهِم مِّنَ ٱلْقُرُونِ
rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God destroyed earlier generations for unbelief and sin; people now walk through their dwellings and see their traces.
rows.anchor: جزاء على كفرهم بالله وارتكابهم لمعاصيه

rows.speaker: قيل
rows.claim: Alternatively, people were destroyed suddenly while absorbed in their own concerns and walking in their homes.
rows.anchor: وقيل: معناه أنا أهلكناهم بغتة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Earlier peoples’ destruction contains clear proofs of truth; disbelievers should listen to admonition.
rows.anchor: أي في إهلاكنا لهم دلالات واضحات على الحق

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God drives water to sterile land through rain and snow; another view says through rivers and springs.
rows.anchor: { أنا نسوق الماء } بالمطر والثلج.

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAbbās says torrents carry water to dry high places in settlements between Syria and Yemen.
rows.anchor: عن ابن عباس

words: فَنُخْرِجُ بِهِۦ زَرْعًۭا تَأْكُلُ مِنْهُ أَنْعَٰمُهُمْ وَأَنفُسُهُمْ
rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Water produces crops for livestock and people, displaying God’s favors.
rows.anchor: والمعنى أن هذه الأرض تنبت ما يأكله الناس والأنعام

rows.speaker: الفراء
rows.claim: Al-Farrāʾ identifies the promised opening as the conquest of Mecca.
rows.anchor: قال الفراء: المراد به فتح مكة

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAbbās transmits from the Prophet: whoever cannot endure the night, fight the enemy, or spend wealth should increase remembrance of God.
rows.anchor: روى ابن عباس عن النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم قال:

rows.speaker: مجاهد
rows.claim: Mujāhid says abundant remembrance means never forgetting God.
rows.anchor: هو أن لا ينساه أبدا عن مجاهد

rows.speaker: قيل
rows.claim: Another view says to remember God by His exalted attributes and beautiful names and declare Him free of what is unfitting.
rows.anchor: وقيل: هو أن يذكره سبحانه بصفاته العلى

rows.speaker: مقاتل
rows.claim: Maqātil says abundant remembrance is saying the four phrases of glorification, praise, unity, and greatness in every circumstance.
rows.anchor: على كل حال عن مقاتل.

rows.speaker: أئمتنا
rows.claim: The Imams say reciting these phrases thirty times counts as abundant remembrance.
rows.anchor: وقد ورد عن أئمتنا ع أنهم قالوا:

rows.speaker: زرارة وحمران عن أبي عبد الله
rows.claim: Zurāra and Ḥumrān ibn Aʿyan transmit from Abū ʿAbd Allāh that the Tasbīḥ of Fāṭima al-Zahrāʾ counts as abundant remembrance.
rows.anchor: وعن زرارة وحمران ابني أعين عن أبي عبد الله ع قال:

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Al-Wāḥidī transmits via al-Ḍaḥḥāk from Ibn ʿAbbās that Gabriel taught a quantified formula of remembrance, promising six merits: abundant remembrance, superiority to ordinary night-and-day remembrance, a tree in Paradise, falling sins, God’s regard, and protection from punishment.
rows.anchor: روى الواحدي بإسناده عن الضحاك بن مزاحم عن ابن عباس قال:

rows.speaker: يعقوب وعبيد بن عمير والأعرج
rows.claim: Yaʿqūb, ʿUbayd ibn ʿUmayr, and al-Aʿraj read al-ṭayr nominative; the other readers read it accusative.
rows.anchor: قرأ يعقوب وعبيد بن عمير والأعرج { والطير } بالرفع

rows.speaker: الزجاج
rows.claim: Al-Zajjāj gives two nominative analyses: birds coordinate with the yāʾ in “repeat,” or with the spoken form “mountains.”
rows.anchor: قال الزجاج: أما الرفع في { والطير } ففيه وجهان

rows.speaker: أبو عبيدة عن أبي عمرو
rows.claim: The accusative can coordinate with “favor,” meaning God granted David a favor and subjected birds to him; it can also be a vocative or mean “with the birds.”
rows.anchor: حكى ذلك أبو عبيدة عن أبي عمرو

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Other accusative analyses coordinate birds with the implied vocative of mountains or take the phrase as “with the birds.”
rows.anchor: والثاني: أن يكون نصبا على النداء

rows.speaker: أبو بكر
rows.claim: Abū Bakr reads al-rīḥ nominative after li-Sulaymān; the rest read it accusative.
rows.anchor: وقرأ أبو بكر { ولسليمان الريح } بالرفع

rows.speaker: أبو علي
rows.claim: The accusative follows “We subjected the wind to him” in 21:81; nominative means Solomon possessed the wind’s subjection, so the sense is equivalent.
rows.anchor: قال أبو علي: من قرأ { ولسليمان الريح } بالنصب

rows.speaker: ابن كثير وأبو عمرو
rows.claim: Ibn Kathīr and Abū ʿAmr retain yāʾ in al-jawābī in connected recitation; at pause Ibn Kathīr retains it and Abū ʿAmr drops it, while others drop it in both positions.
rows.anchor: قرأ ابن كثير وأبو عمرو كالجوابي بالياء في الوصل

rows.speaker: أبو علي
rows.claim: The expected form retains yāʾ with the article; Abū ʿAmr drops it at pause as a verse-end delimiter, and other readers delete it by a common pattern.
rows.anchor: والقياس في الجوابي أن يثبت الياء مع الألف واللام

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Medinese, Abū ʿAmr, Ibn Fulayḥ, and Zayd from Yaʿqūb read without hamza; Ibn ʿĀmir has a vowelless hamza and the rest a fatḥa hamza.
rows.anchor: قرأ أهل المدينة وأبو عمرو وابن فليح وزيد عن يعقوب { منسأته } بغير همز

rows.speaker: يعقوب
rows.claim: Yaʿqūb reads tabayyanat al-jinn with ḍamma on tāʾ and bāʾ and kasra on yāʾ; others open all three.
rows.anchor: وقرأ يعقوب تبينت الجن بضم التاء والباء وكسر الياء

rows.speaker: ابن عباس والضحاك وعلي بن الحسين وأبو عبد الله
rows.claim: A noncanonical reading, also attributed to ʿAlī Zayn al-ʿĀbidīn and Abū ʿAbd Allāh, says “the humans realized”; it is in ʿAbd Allāh’s codex and conveys that jinn lacked unseen knowledge.
rows.anchor: وفي الشواذ قراءة ابن عباس والضحاك تبينت الإنس

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Taʾwīb means repeated return in glorification; Salāma ibn Jandal’s verse uses it for going back and forth.
rows.anchor: التأويب الترجيع بالتسبيح قال سلامة بن جندل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Sābigh means ample or complete clothing; sard of iron means ordering its links, from the sense of following one part of speech after another.
rows.anchor: والسابغ التام من اللباس وسرد الحديد نظمه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: An unattributed poem describes a sound, tightly woven coat of mail; Abū Dhuʾayb describes two coats of mail made by David or by armor makers.
rows.anchor: وقال أبو ذؤيب: وعليهما مسرودتان قضاهما داود

rows.speaker: المبرد
rows.claim: Al-Mubarrad says a miḥrāb is only a structure reached by climbing steps; verses by ʿAdī ibn Zayd and Waḍḍāḥ al-Yaman illustrate the term.
rows.anchor: قال المبرد: لا يسمى محرابا إلا ما يرتقى إليه بدرج

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Tamāthīl are images or statues; singular timthāl derives from standing upright, as something is set up standing.
rows.anchor: والتماثيل صور الأشياء واحدها تمثال

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A Prophetic report warns that whoever wants people to stand for him should take his seat in the Fire.
rows.anchor: من سره أن يمثل له الناس فليتبوء مقعده من النار

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Jawābī is the plural of jābiya, a great basin that collects water; al-Aʿshā compares an overflowing dish to an Iraqi elder’s basin.
rows.anchor: والجوابي جمع جابية وهي الحوض العظيم
